article.title: From Prediction to Decision: The Economics of Model Thresholds
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: A classification model often produces a probability or score rather than a final business action. The action appears only after someone chooses a threshold. Customers above the threshold may receive an offer, transactions may be sent for fraud review, or applications may require additional checks. Although threshold selection is sometimes presented as a purely technical task, it is fundamentally an economic and operational decision. Consider a binary classifier with false positives and false negatives. Their costs are rarely symmetric. In fraud detection, a false negative may allow a costly fraudulent transaction, while a false positive may inconvenience a legitimate customer and consume review capacity. In marketing, contacting a customer who would not respond has a small delivery cost but may also create fatigue. Failing to contact a persuadable customer sacrifices incremental profit. A threshold should therefore reflect the value and cost of possible actions, not merely maximize F1 score. Precision and recall describe useful statistical trade-offs, but neither specifies what an error is worth. The same model can rationally use different thresholds in different businesses or even different customer segments if economics and constraints differ. Capacity makes the problem more concrete. Suppose an operations team can manually review only ten thousand cases per day. Even if a lower threshold would identify more true positives, the organization cannot act on all of them. Ranking quality near the operational cutoff may then matter more than performance across the entire score distribution. Calibration also matters when expected-value calculations use predicted probabilities. A model can rank cases well while systematically overestimating risk. If decisions multiply predicted probability by financial impact, poor calibration can lead to the wrong threshold even with a strong AUC. Decision analysis should define the available actions, expected outcomes under each action, intervention costs, opportunity costs, and constraints. For a simple case, act when the expected incremental benefit exceeds the expected incremental cost. In practice, these quantities can depend on treatment effect rather than outcome propensity. A customer with a high purchase probability is not necessarily the customer with the highest incremental response to an offer. This is why a predictive score and a decision policy should not be treated as the same object. Thresholds also interact with prevalence. When the base rate changes, precision can change even if sensitivity and specificity remain stable. A threshold chosen on last year’s population may therefore produce a very different workload or positive predictive value this year. Monitoring should track not only model metrics but also action volume, downstream conversion, unit economics, and capacity utilization. Fairness or policy constraints can further restrict acceptable decision rules. Certain thresholds may create disparate operational outcomes across groups, requiring governance beyond profit maximization. The threshold itself should be versioned and documented like other decision logic. Teams should record why it was chosen, what cost assumptions were used, what capacity existed, and when it should be reviewed. Scenario analysis is often more useful than searching for a single mathematically optimal point. Show how profit, recall, workload, complaints, or other outcomes change across plausible thresholds. Decision makers can then see the trade-offs explicitly. Machine learning creates value only when predictions lead to better actions. The model estimates something about the world; the threshold determines how the organization responds. Treating threshold selection as an economic decision closes the gap between predictive performance and business value. Analysts should state the population, denominator, observation window, and decision rule before interpreting the result. A useful review separates the observed metric from the mechanism that produced it and from the action that should follow. This makes the conclusion easier to reproduce, challenge, and communicate. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文強調，指標本身不足以支撐決策。解讀百分比、彙總結果、model drift、非顯著結果或分類 threshold 時，都必須同時確認母體、分母、比較基準、統計不確定性以及實際 business cost。只有把觀察結果與資料生成機制、決策條件分開，才能避免過度解讀。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：percentage、集計値、model drift、非有意な結果、classification thresholdは、数値だけでは意思決定を支えられない。母集団、分母、比較基準、統計的不確実性、business costを確認し、観察結果とdata generating mechanism、decision ruleを分けて解釈する必要がある。
